claims.text: A representative target system is a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni high-entropy alloy.
The target alloy is evaluated near its melting transition.
A modest ab initio molecular-dynamics dataset sampled at key temperatures in both solid and liquid phases can be used to train an MLIP.
The trained MLIP can be combined with accelerated sampling to perform thermodynamic integration.
The proposed method is applicable to quinary high-entropy alloys from ambient temperature to approximately 2000 K, including temperatures above melting.
An interatomic potential can provide a computational representation of an Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy that agrees with first-principles calculations for at least some properties.
An MLIP trained on ab initio configurations embeds the quantum effects needed to describe electron-vibration coupling.
An MLIP trained on ab initio configurations embeds the anharmonic contributions needed for phase free energies.
The quality of the trained MLIP governs the accuracy of free-energy integration across solid and liquid phases.
A sparse ab initio molecular-dynamics dataset captures the critical electronic interactions required for the calculation.
A sparse ab initio molecular-dynamics dataset captures the critical anharmonic interactions required for the calculation.
The MLIP efficiently interpolates the relevant potential-energy surface.
Accelerated sampling reduces the trajectory lengths needed to integrate phase free energies accurately.
The combined workflow preserves free-energy fidelity in both solid and liquid phases.
The method will produce phase free energies within approximately 2-3 meV/atom of explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics results.
The method will reduce computational time by roughly an order of magnitude relative to TOR-TILD and full ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows.
The method's accuracy depends critically on the representativeness of the ab initio training set and the transferability of the MLIP.
Al0.1CrCoFeNi can serve as the quinary benchmark alloy.
A deviation exceeding approximately 3 meV/atom in either solid- or liquid-phase free energy relative to explicit ab initio MD or TOR-TILD would falsify the hypothesis.
Significant disagreement in entropy, heat capacity, or fusion enthalpy would indicate loss of fidelity in the relevant entropy and coupling effects.
